newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Prices mean Brazil coffee growers clean the closet.
newsitem.headline: Prices mean Brazil coffee growers clean the closet.

text.p: High prices and a stable currency are encouraging Brazil's coffee producers to sell their stocks at a rate which has not been seen in recent years.
"Producers are selling a lot of coffee. I have never seen such sales," said Manoel Bertone, vice-president of the National Coffee Council which represents growers.
"We supposedly don't have coffee and yet we're shipping like crazy. Producers are cleaning the closets," one trader said.
In other years, producers tended to hold back coffee even when prices were very good, according to an article published in the monthly newsletter of the Garcafe cooperative in Sao Paulo.

"This bore evidence to the practice of saving using coffee, perhaps due to poor faith in the currency because of high inflation. Today, with a stable currency, good prices are leading to a complete unloading of stocks," it added.
Cooperative sales in February reached 748,812 60-kg bags, up from 720,579 in January and almost exactly twice the 324,734 bags sold in February last year.
While understandably higher than last year's sales from drought and frost-hit harvest, this year's levels were also substantially above those of February 1994.
"Even some 'coffee collectors' as those people are called who keep product from various crops, are selling considerable amounts, cleaning out the barns," the Garcafe newsletter said.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries, which today published its latest production estimates, noted the presence of old crop coffee amongst exports and the addition of government stock sales which could be leading to overestimates of the 1996/97 crop.
Bertone, who is also president of the Garcafe cooperative, said he knew of sales of coffee from harvests in 1995, 1994 and even 1992.
Prices were around 30 to 40 reais a bag below normal levels for current crop coffee but these sales were now coming to an end, he said.
One obvious result of the higher sales has been a drop in stocks. As of March 19, 180 producers within the Garca cooperative were holding stocks totalling 59,970 bags.
Of these, 14,936 bags were being held by 154 producers, 10,460 bags by 14 producers and 34,574 bags by 12 producers.
The same pattern of a small number of producers holding a larg percentage of total stocks was seen in the affiliated Patrocinio cooperative were stocks by March 19 were 71,592 bags.
"Throughout this year, we have received coffee from 975 producers, of which only 328 (34 percent) possessed coffee at the time of the survey," the Garca newsletter said.
"Only 26...of these producers were responsible for 63 percent of the stock in a clear demonstration of a concentration of stocks in the hands of the largest and strongest producers," it added.

One other booster to the current crop has been government auctions, with the government due to hold its biggest sale so far this crop year of just over 300,000 bags open to the whole sector on April 2.
A further 25,915 bags are to be put on offer just for the soluble industry.

Exporter participation in previous auctions has been reasonably small but rose to around 20 percent in last month's sale, with most of the coffee going to the domestic roasting industry, Bertone said.
If the price of coffee continues to rise, producers would not object to larger quantities being offered to the market in the immediate future although not more than 50,000 bags more, Bertone said.
"If the prices carry on rising, I think we can accept higher auctions. We have to respect the customer," he said.
((Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
